title: Growth Rate
text: “And, well, that about covers it, I say.”
That day, I was teaching Father the written language of this world. First up was the official language of Melromarc, naturally.
“I see… so according to Motoyasu-kun, even weapon skills don’t come with automatic literacy?”
“Indeed. Even I, who’ve been through countless loops, have never once seen ‘Otherworld Script Comprehension’ as a skill, I say.”

If only text could be translated automatically like speech, but that particular convenience simply never existed. From conversations with Ark and the spirit of the spear, I could now guess at the reason to some extent. Written characters, unlike spoken words, likely vary too much by region and era for any single system to account for them all. Spoken language, I believe, gets conveyed through the weapon acting as a kind of intermediary for the speaker’s intent. Writing, being an extra layer—a cushion, so to speak—between intent and understanding, must be far harder to bridge.
“That sounds rough. I’m not exactly a genius, and I’m bad at memorizing things unless I really need to.”
“Not to worry. Every version of Father across every world eventually learns to read, I say.”

In every loop, Father always ended up mastering the written word eventually. Interestingly, which script he learned depended on which country he ended up in. The Father who went to Siltvelt, for instance, naturally picked up Siltvelt’s writing system. Father might be modest about it, but he really does have a good memory, I say. Compare that to certain pigs I’ve taught, who barely scraped by no matter how many times I went over the material—absolute fools who’d forget everything within three days. Next to that, a Father who actually retains what he’s taught is downright a joy to instruct.
“It’s thanks to how well you teach, Motoyasu-kun, that I’ve managed to pick up as much as I have. Honestly, it surprises even me.”
“The other-loop Fathers analyzed it before—apparently, even without direct translation of the script, the words themselves get remembered mentally, I say.”
“Ah, I see. So if you memorize it by ear, the characters naturally start coming to mind too, maybe?”
“Indeed.”
“In that case, I guess I should pay more attention to whatever language everyone in this circus is using too.”
Since we were technically still within Melromarc’s borders, the Siltvelt envoy had apparently been speaking to Father in Melromarc’s language as a courtesy.
“Woof?”
Wolf came trotting over, sniffing curiously at Father, who was in the middle of his studies.
“I wonder which country’s language Wolf actually understands.”
“Woof? Vow!”
Wolf barked as if to say he didn’t really know either.
“I can manage everyday conversation to some degree myself, but when it comes to the written word, it’s a constant study session,” Rabbit Guy said.

Sitting in on Father’s writing lessons that day were also Rabbit Guy and the half-breed Lizardman. Incidentally, Rabbit Guy apparently had poor eyesight, so Father had bought him a pair of glasses, which he now wore during study sessions.
“Theo, do you follow the spoken language okay?”
“To some degree… yes. I was dragged around to a lot of different countries growing up, so I picked things up naturally.”
“I see…”
“Looks like Sion can read Melromarc’s script just fine.”
“Ah… well, I’m originally from this country, so a bit, yeah.”

The half-breed Lizardman was checking over Rabbit Guy’s practice problems. It seemed that once Rabbit Guy had shown interest in joining the lessons, Father had invited him in, and somewhere along the way the half-breed Lizardman had started helping correct his work too. Rabbit Guy learned quickly, and his arithmetic had improved considerably. I was pitching in with some teaching myself, and honestly, his learning ability seemed quite sharp. His grasp of writing had been shaky at first, but lately he’d gotten good at calculations too. Apparently Rabbit Guy could already read to some extent, but when we had him write out what he could read, it turned out to be Siltvelt-region script. Though according to the Siltvelt envoy, there were some odd, accented spellings mixed in—more characteristic, apparently, of the Shieldfreeden dialect. So now Rabbit Guy was relearning Melromarc’s script from scratch.
“I understand the spoken word well enough, but writing is another matter entirely. It’s quite the struggle,” Rabbit Guy said with a wry laugh.

Both the half-breed Lizardman and Big Sister could understand spoken Melromarc but had little grasp of other countries’ languages. Older Sister and Panda, on the other hand, could understand other languages just fine. Seemed like the language barrier existed in every world. Incidentally, Rabbit Guy was apparently also eager to pick up magic, practicing whenever he had a spare moment. While the half-breed Lizardman trained in combat against me, Elephant, Wolf, and Older Sister, Rabbit Guy would be off studying spellcraft on the side. Hmm… if I recalled correctly, he used to fight with a dagger—perhaps he was considering switching up his combat style. Lately, Father had been remarking on how much the half-breed Lizardman’s combat skills had improved. Watching their practice sessions, I could indeed feel his fighting style growing more polished by the day, though he still had a ways to go. Rabbit Guy, by contrast, wasn’t nearly as proactive about combat training. Well, no—he did seem to be training on his own quietly while everyone else slept, but he just wasn’t showing much growth from it. I’d spotted him more than once running laps around the tent or doing push-ups, presumably trying to build up stamina. That reminded me, actually… of the scene I’d witnessed with Big Sister back when we did that party-swap on Cal Mira Island. Father seemed to have noticed as well, since he’d been checking everyone’s status stats. He shared with me that among the slaves, Wolf’s stats were unsurprisingly high, and the half-breed Lizardman’s had grown considerably too, but Rabbit Guy’s stat gains from leveling up lagged behind the other two. So the thinking was that Rabbit Guy was probably searching for other ways to make himself useful. As for his magical aptitude, apparently it leaned toward all-around support-type magic across every element. Being unspecialized meant it was the sort of trait that was hard to develop into a real strength—quite the troublesome aptitude, honestly. He supposedly had some offensive aptitude too, but weaker than a typical all-elemental type. Combined with the poor stat growth from leveling, it was a magical aptitude that sounded oddly familiar somehow.
“Well then… let’s take a short break.”
“Yes.”
At Father’s well-timed suggestion, the half-breed Lizardman and I set about grading papers.
“Phew…”
Father, apparently using the break to check on the slaves’ stats again.

“I’ll go do a bit of magic practice, then,” Rabbit Guy said, flipping through a spellbook procured by the Siltvelt envoy. He then moved on to practicing conjuring magic from his fingertips. A small flame flickered to life at the tip of his finger. He went on practicing water, wind, and earth magic as well, though his magical power seemed quite low.
“…Lately you’ve been all about magic and barely doing any combat training,” the half-breed Lizardman muttered at Rabbit Guy.
“No matter how hard I try, I’ll always be a step behind Sion, so I want to build up other options I can rely on. I already know, after all… my stat growth from leveling isn’t great, is it?”
Rabbit Guy asked Father, as if seeking confirmation. Father hesitated for a moment over how to answer, then nodded with a somewhat wry smile.
“…Yeah. Compared to Sion and Wolf, Theo’s stat growth from leveling up isn’t… great, no.”
The half-breed Lizardman fell silent, looking somewhat displeased as he continued grading papers, glancing over at Rabbit Guy’s wry smile.
“That said, your rate of leveling itself is actually pretty good, Theo. Might be that you just need less experience to level up than usual.”
